content: Chondrolectin is a protein encoded by the CHODL gene in humans, while in mice, it is encoded by the Chodl gene. Chondrolectin is classified as a type I membrane protein. Its extracellular region contains a carbohydrate recognition domain, which is a defining feature of C-type lectins. In other proteins, this domain plays a role in the endocytosis of glycoproteins and sugar-bearing pathogens of external origin. Chondrolectin has been observed to localize near the perinuclear region of cells. The precise biological function of chondrolectin remains unclear. However, it has been identified as a marker for fast motor neurons in mice. In zebrafish (Danio rerio), it is implicated in the development and growth of motor neurons. In humans, chondrolectin has been found to localize specifically to motor neurons within the spinal cord. Chondrolectin has clinical relevance in the context of spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), a neuromuscular disorder that primarily affects lower motor neurons. In mouse models of SMA, the CHODL gene undergoes alternative splicing in the spinal cord. In zebrafish models of SMA, elevated levels of chondrolectin have been associated with significant improvements in motor neuron defects related to the disease.
